 Daylight saving time expected to end Nov. 1 as Trump demands Congress pass legislation
 BY 
 Erin Pflaumer
 Washington, D.C. 
 PUBLISHED 5:45 PM ET Oct. 30, 2026 
 PUBLISHED 5:45 PM EDT Oct. 30, 2026 
 SHARE 
 Daylight saving time will once again end on Nov. 1 as the Senate isn't expected to vote on a bill this year that would make it permanent.
 The legislation, named the Sunshine Protection Act, was passed by the House in July in a 308-117 vote. Supporters argued that it gives Americans more daylight during the hours they're most active.
 "Permanent daylight saving time will improve public safety, promote healthier and more active lifestyles and give families more daylight to enjoy after work and school," the bill's sponsor, Florida Republican Rep. Vern Buchanan, said.
 Buchanan has introduced the legislation in the House every year since 2018. Congress previously enacted a trial period for daylight saving time during the 1973 energy crisis, which would last from January 1974 to April 1975, but it was later repealed and standard time returned by October 1974.
 Nineteen states have already passed proposals to enact permanent daylight saving time if Congress passes the legislation. Those states include Texas, Oklahoma, Colorado, Alabama, Georgia, Minnesota, Mississippi, Montana, Idaho, Louisiana, South Carolina, Utah, Wyoming, Delaware, Maine, Oregon, Tennessee, Washington and Florida, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
 But the states cannot act unless Congress takes action.
 "The United States Senate is letting the Daylight Saving Bill die, when a vast Majority of the Country want it. Most people are demanding light in the evening, but ALL want not to change their clocks anymore. TAKE A VOTE!" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Oct. 26.
 In early October, the president leaked the personal cellphone number of Republican Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, a staunch opponent of the bill.
 "No one likes changing the clock, me included, but Congress has enacted permanent Daylight Savings Time multiple times before and repealed it each time once Americans experienced absurdly late sunrises in the winter. Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first," Cotton wrote on Facebook after his phone number was revealed.
 Critics of the legislation said it would lead to some states not seeing sunshine until 9 a.m. There are also concerns about children traveling to school in the dark if daylight saving time became permanent.
 In an AP-NORC poll from last October, only 12% of Americans liked the current daylight saving time system, 47% were opposed and 40% were neutral.
 Daylight saving time requires people in most states to change their clocks twice a year. Arizona and Hawaii are the only two states that have enacted permanent standard time.
 The Associated Press contributed to this report.
